Tidal locking, a phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, profoundly shapes planetary climates in ways that challenge our Earth-centric assumptions about habitability.

The most dramatic examples orbit red dwarf stars, the most common stars in our galaxy. Planets close enough to these dim stars to maintain liquid water become tidally locked, with one hemisphere in perpetual daylight and the other in eternal night. This creates one of the most extreme temperature contrasts imaginable: the dayside of a locked planet can reach 2,000°C while the nightside plunges to -200°C, a difference exceeding anything in our solar system.

Yet tidal locking doesn't necessarily preclude habitability.
